B.5 Specter: linear deconvolution as a new paradigm for targeted analysis of data-independent acquisition mass spectrometry proteomics Ryan Peckner1, Samuel A. Myers1, Jarrett D. Egertson2, Richard S. Johnson2, Steven A. Carr1, Michael J. MacCoss2, Jacob D. Jaffe1 1The Broad Institute of of MIT and Harvard, Cambridge, MA, USA; 2University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA Mass spectrometry with data-independent acquisition (DIA) has emerged as a promising method to greatly improve the comprehensiveness and reproducibility of targeted and discovery proteomics, in theory systematically measuring all peptide precursors within a biological sample. Despite the technical maturity of DIA, the analytical challenges involved in discriminating between peptides with similar sequences in convoluted spectra have limited its applicability in important cases, such as the detection of single-nucleotide polymorphisms and alternative site localizations in phosphoproteomics data. We have developed Specter, an open-source software tool that uses linear algebra to deconvolute DIA mixture spectra directly in terms of a spectral library, circumventing the problems associated with typical fragment correlation-based approaches. We validate the sensitivity of Specter and its performance relative to other methods by means of several complex datasets, and show that Specter is able to successfully analyze cases involving highly similar peptides that are typically challenging for DIA analysis methods. B.6 Targeting RAS Driven Cancers with Antibodies to Upregulated and Functionally Important Cell-Surface Proteins Alexander J. Martinko1, Charles Truillet1, Olivier Julien1, Juan A. Diaz1, Max Horlbeck1, Gordon Whiteley2, Josip Blonder2, Jonathan Weissman1, Sourav Bandyopadhyay1, Michael Evans1, James A. Wells1 1University of California, San Francisco, CA, USA; 2Frederick National Laboratory for Cancer Research, Frederick, MD, USA While there have been tremendous efforts to target oncogenic RAS signaling from inside the cell, little effort has focused on the cell-surface. Using quantitative surface proteomics, we discovered a signature of proteins critical for metastasis that are upregulated on cells transformed with KRASG12V, and driven by MAPK pathway signaling. We next generated a toolkit of recombinant antibodies to several RAS induced membrane proteins. We show that five of these targets are broadly distributed on cancer cell lines harboring KRAS mutations. In parallel, a cell-surface CRISPRi screen identified integrin and Wnt signaling proteins as critical to RAS transformed cells. We demonstrate that antibodies to CDCP1, a protein identified by both efforts, can be leveraged to deliver cytotoxic and immunotherapeutic payloads to RAS transformed cancer cells and report for RAS signaling status in vivo. This compendium of data and recombinant antibodies provides a rich resource for approaching a new paradigm of attacking RAS from outside the cell. B.7 Defining Kinase Inhibitor Polypharmacology with Multiplexed Inhibitor Bead Proteomics: Abemaciclib Inhibits Glycogen Synthase Kinase 3 Beta to Activate WNT Signaling Emily M. Cousins, Dennis Goldfarb, Feng Yan, Jose Roques, David Darr, Gary L. Johnson, Michael B. Major University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, NC, USA The cellular and organismal phenotypic response to a small molecule kinase inhibitor is defined collectively by its targets and their functions. Kinase inhibitor polypharmacology—the study of all targets for a given drug—promises to improve drug repurposing efforts and better inform the management of drug toxicities. We leveraged a competitive kinase enrichment proteomics approach using live cells and mice to define the polypharmacology landscape for several clinically active kinase inhibitors, including trametinib, BMS-777607, dasatinib, erlotinib, abemaciclib, ribociclib, and palbociclib. MIB/MS competition analyses of the cyclin-dependent kinase 4 and 6 (CDK4/6) inhibitors abemaciclib, palbociclib and ribociclib revealed overlapping and unique kinase targets. We show that in contrast to palbociclib and ribociclib, abemaciclib directly inhibits glycogen synthase kinase 3 beta (GSK3β) kinase activity with an IC50 of 8.67 nM. Consequently, abemaciclib activates β-catenin-dependent WNT signaling, as determined by β-catenin transcriptional activation and β-catenin protein stabilization. These data reveal differential kinase target specificities for CDK4/6 inhibitors that may govern clinical efficacy and dose-limiting toxicities in patients treated with these drugs. More broadly, we highlight the use of an unbiased MIB/MS-based chemical proteomics technology in live cells and in mice to identify targets of kinase inhibitors. B.8 Large-scale phosphoproteomics reveals Shp2 phosphatase-dependent regulators of Pdgf receptor signaling Tanveer S. Batth1, Moreno Papetti1, Anamarija Pfeiffer1, Chiara Francavilla2, Jesper V. Olsen1 1NNF Center for Protein Research, Copenhagen, Denmark; 2University of Manchester, Manchester, UK Tyrosine phosphorylation (pTyr) regulates numerous cell signaling pathways in health and disease. However, its detection and quantitation remains challenging due to its low cellular abundance. We applied comprehensive phosphoproteomics to unravel differential regulators of receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) initiated signaling networks upon activation by Pdgf-ββ, Fgf-2 or Igf-1, respectively, and identified over 40,000 phosphorylation sites. The analysis revealed RTK-specific regulation of hundreds of tyrosine phosphorylation sites on key adaptor and signaling molecules. We found the tyrosine phosphatase Shp2 to be the master regulator of Pdgfr pTyr signaling. Application of a recently-introduced allosteric Shp2 inhibitor revealed global regulation of the Pdgf-dependent tyrosine phosphoproteome, which significantly altered the interaction of Pdgfr with signaling proteins and impaired cell migration but not cell proliferation. We present a list of hundreds of Shp2-dependent targets and putative substrates including Rasa1 and Cortactin with increased tyrosine phosphorylation, and Gab1 and Erk1/2 with decreased tyrosine phosphorylation. Our study demonstrates that large-scale quantitative phosphoproteomics can precisely dissect tightly regulated kinase/phosphatase signaling networks. B.9 Identification of Predictive Biomarkers For Radiation Injury From Circulating Serum And Urine Exosomes Emily Chen1, A. Ribault2, S. Kulkarni3, A. Koller4 1Columbia University Medical Center, New York, NY, USA; 2Institut de Radioprotection et de Sûreté Nucléaire Fontenay-aux-Roses, France; 3Department of Radiation Oncology, Albert Einstein College of Medicine, Bronx, NY, USA; 4Proteomics Shared Resource at the Herbert Irving Comprehensive Cancer Center, CUMC, New York, NY, USA Exosomes are cell-derived vesicles that carry a wide range of molecules including genetic material, proteins and lipids as their cargos. We hypothesize that comprehensive characterization of urine and serum exosomes in response to radiation exposure at various radiation doses and times could lead to a panel of biomarkers that could be used as (i) biodosimetry tool to determine radiation injury and (ii) pharmacodynamic parameter for radio-mitigation screening to quantitatively assess the extent of mitigation. In our recent studies, we analyzed circulating exosomes from serum and urine samples collected from a WBI mouse model and serum exosome collected from a group of patients who underwent pelvic radiation therapy and developed various degrees of acute toxicity in response to radiation. Using quantitative mass spectrometry-based proteomics technology and statistical analyses with a B-H FDR correction, we detected and quantified 321 proteins from urine exosome and 674 proteins from serum exosome. From the human cohort, we detected and quantified 547 proteins from serum exosome. For the WBI mouse model study, we identified 23 biomarkers from urine and 24 biomarkers from serum exosomes indicative of radiation-induced injury. Urinary exosome signatures identified different physiological parameters than the ones obtained in serum exosomes. Exosome signatures from urine indicated injury to the liver, gastrointestinal, and genitourinary tracts. In contrast, serum showed vascular injuries and acute inflammation in response to radiation. For the human cohort study, we identified 71 biomarkers that correlate with 3 grades of radiation-induced toxicity. Furthermore, among biomarkers associated with high grade of radiation-induced toxicity, 6 of these proteins were also found in the radiation injury signature we identified from the WBI mouse model. Together, these data showed the feasibility of defining biomarkers that could elucidate tissue-associated and systemic response caused by ionizing radiation. This is the first report using an exosome proteomics approach to identify signatures of radiation-induced injury. B.10 Quantitative comparison of the O-GlcNAcome in Female and Male Embryonic Stem Cells Jason C. Maynard1, Elizabeth Allene Martin2, Barbara Panning2, A. L. Burlingame1 Departments of 1Pharmaceutical Chemistry, 2Department of Biochemistry and Biophysics, University of California, San Francisco, CA, USA DNA methylation occurring at the 5′ position of cytosines is a key epigenetic regulator of mammalian embryogenesis and stem cell differentiation. Levels of 5-methylcytosine (5mC) are determined by DNMT and TET proteins. DNMTs add methyl groups to CpG dinucleotides to generate 5mC, while TET proteins catalyze oxidation of 5mC to 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC). 5hmC can lead to demethylation by iterative TET-mediated oxidation and base excision repair. Female mouse embryonic stem cells (ESCs) have dramatically reduced levels of 5mC relative to male ESCs. This reduction is unique to ESCs, which have two active X chromosomes, unlike somatic cells, since X-inactivation equalizes gene dosage between sexes. These results suggest the two-fold increase in expression of X-linked genes direct hypomethylation in XX ESCs. A candidate for this X-linked gene is Ogt, which encodes O-GlcNAc transferase. Female ESCs produce twice as much OGT as males; and OGT directly interacts with and modifies TET proteins. We sought to determine whether OGT modifies more unique proteins involved in the DNA methylation pathway in female ESCs compared to males. We have enriched for O-GlcNAc modified peptides using lectin weak affinity chromatography and quantitatively assessed the O-GlcNAcome of male and female embryonic stem cells using SILAC based mass spectrometry approaches. B.11 Investigation of novel MELK interacting proteins and signaling pathways in triple-negative breast cancer Ian M. McDonald, Raquel C. Martinez Chacin, Xianxi Wang, Laura E. Herring, Michael J. Emanuele, Lee M. Graves University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, NC, USA In women, breast cancer is the most commonly occurring type of cancer, and the second leading cause of cancer deaths. Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) accounts for 12–17% of all breast cancers. Patients with TNBC have markedly lower survival rates than those with other breast cancer subtypes, partially due to a lack of effective targeted therapies. Notably, MELK (Maternal Embryonic Leucine zipper Kinase) has recently been implicated in TNBC, along with other difficult to treat cancers. Increased MELK expression in TNBC is correlated with radioresistance, tumor grade, and poor prognosis. Correspondingly, MELK depletion slows proliferation of both TNBC cells and xenografts, and sensitizes them to radiation. Finally, the compound OTSSP167, developed as a MELK inhibitor, is currently in phase 1/2 clinical trials for solid tumors, TNBC, and leukemia, demonstrating significant therapeutic interest in this kinase. Remarkably, the precise function of MELK in cancer is poorly understood. MELK has been implicated in varied processes, including cell cycle progression, cancer stem cell phenotype, and protein translation. Specifically, evidence suggests that in mitosis MELK phosphorylates and activates FoxM1, an oncogenic transcription factor and master regulator of mitotic genes. However, the phosphorylation site has not been determined and mechanisms underlying increased FoxM1 transcriptional activity following phosphorylation by MELK have not been elucidated. Using mass spectrometry (MS), I have identified Ser481 of FoxM1 as a putative MELK phosphorylation site. In collaboration with the Emanuele Lab, FoxM1-S481D and -S481E phosphomimetic mutants were found to have increased activity using a FoxM1 reporter assay. Experiments to further validate and determine the mechanistic effects of this phosphorylation are ongoing. In addition to the FoxM1 relationship, there is a clear need for further investigation into the function and regulation of MELK to elucidate its importance in cancer. To date, few MELK substrates have been definitively validated. The identification of kinase substrates by co-IP can be difficult due to the transient nature of phosphorylation events. One alternative to this approach is proximity-dependent biotin identification, or BioID. This technique utilizes a promiscuous biotin ligase (BirA*) fused to a protein of interest to irreversibly biotinylate proximal proteins in cells, and ultimately detect them by MS. Preliminary BioID experiments using an N-terminal BirA*-MELK fusion protein identified numerous cell cycle-related putative MELK interactors, including CDK1/cyclin B, the MCM complex (MCM2–7), and p53. Efforts to validate these proteins as bona fide MELK interactors, and to determine the nature of these interactions, are ongoing. Additionally, phosphoproteomics and multiplexed inhibitor beads/mass spectrometry (MIB/MS) will be used as complementary approaches to better understand relevant MELK signaling pathways in TNBC. B.12 Characterizing the inducible degradation of mutant PIK3CA using mass spectrometry Lilian Phu, Kyle A. Edgar, Kyung Song, William Forrest, Lori Friedman, Donald S. Kirkpatrick Genentech, South San Francisco, CA, USA Phosphotidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) is one of the most frequently altered signaling pathways in cancer. Mutations in the PIK3CA gene, which encodes the p110alpha subunit of class IA PI3K enzymes, are transforming and result in increased kinase activity and activation of downstream signaling. We have discovered that the PI3K inhibitor, Taselisib (GDC-0032), a novel, oral, selective inhibitor of p110alpha, sparing inhibition of p110beta, is more potent against cancer cells bearing mutations in the PIK3CA gene than those with wild-type PIK3CA. Taselisib treatment induces more apoptotic cell death in PIK3CA mutant cancer cells in comparison to other PI3K inhibitors. Taselisib has a dual mechanism of action, both blocking PI3K kinase signaling, and resulting in a decrease in p110alpha protein levels. To better understand the effect of Taselisib on p110alpha, an approach to quantify the levels of wild-type versus mutant p110alpha was desired. Quantification of each form via immunoblotting was not possible since cell lines harboring PIK3CA mutations are heterozygous and current antibodies against p110alpha cannot distinguish between wild-type and mutant p110alpha. Therefore, a mass spectrometric approach was applied to quantify levels of each type of p110alpha (WT vs. mutant). MS analysis revealed that Taselisib treatment leads to the specific depletion of mutant p110alpha without significant change in the wild-type protein. B.13 High throughput proteomics approach reveals mechanistic basis of acute viral pathogenesis mediated by an RNAi suppressor protein in insect cells Arabinda Nayak1, Michael J. Trnka1, Kathy Li1, Craig Kerr2, Eric Jan2, A. L. Burlingame1, Raul Andino1 1University of California, San Francisco, CA, USA; 2University of British Columbia, Vancouver, BC, Canada Confronted with viral pathogens, insects use RNA interference (RNAi) to defend themselves. Accordingly, viral RNAi suppressors engage insect RNAi immunity and modulate viral pathogenesis. Cricket Paralysis Virus (CrPV) infects a broad range of insects and causes acute infections in both Drosophila and mosquito cells in contrast to the majority of the insect viruses, which cause persistent infections. Hence, CrPV provided an ideal platform to interrogate the molecular components of insect immunity that fight virus infection and dissect viral mechanisms that mediate either acute or persistent infections in insects. Burlingame1 1University of California, San Francisco, CA, USA; 2Alkahest, San Carlos, CA, USA Biological systems are modulated at the protein level by a variety of different mechanisms, in many cases involving posttranslational modification (PTM) of particular residues on polypeptides; PTMs affect and regulate the activities of the polypeptides in myriad ways – many of which are yet to be defined and are certainly not understood functionally. Due to the inherent sub-stoichiometric nature of PTMs, PTM-containing peptides are grossly under-sampled in proteomic analysis of digests from complex biological mixtures. Detection and identification of these relatively low abundance peptides, present in a matrix of abundant non-modified components, is a challenging task. To address this problem, strategies for selective enrichment of different types of PTM-containing peptides have been developed. The dotation of PTMs is dynamic in nature; simultaneous changes can occur in different PTMs over the same or different sets of proteins involved on the same process or signaling pathway, with stimulatory or inhibitory modifications of different origin (phosphorylation, acetylation, ubiquitylation,…). Thus, in order to have clear molecular level details of the signaling events, development of optimized multi-stage PTM enrichment strategies is critical for providing a comprehensive view of the cellular state and understanding the complexity of signaling networks in cells. Recently a protocol has been reported based on integrating sequential purification steps for phosphorylated, ubiquitylated and acetylated peptide components from the same sample, followed by MS analysis (Mertins P, et al. Integrated proteomic analysis of post-translational modifications by serial enrichment. Nat Methods. 2013 Jul;10(7):634–637). We are performing experiments to design an optimized protocol to perform sequential enrichments of these and additional enrichment techniques for different PTMs (S/T and Y phosphorylation, O-GlcNAcylation, acetylation, ubiquitylation). We are using tryptic digests obtained from SILAC labelled cellular extracts to assess the effects of the order of different PTM enrichment techniques (TiO2 chromatography for phosphorylation, IP for acetylation, ubiquitination and tyrosine phosphorylation, lectin affinity for O-GlcNAc), and of selective removal competing modified species (PNGaseF pretreatment) on the recovery efficiency of the different modified species. Additional criteria for evaluation of the success of the different protocols include total number of peptides found, and selectivity assessed by percentage of modified species in the fractions collected. The large parameter space that must be explored in order to unite different enrichment methods in a sequential manner is the main challenge in this endeavor. In order to be able to explore such a space of possible configurations, we are exploring binomial combinations and restricting the number of initial configurations to consider by making some reasonable assumptions (i.e., all immunoaffinity based techniques should be done consecutively, since this would minimize buffer substitutions). Successful integration will arise also from minimizing losses of material in the different steps due to extended handling, buffer and solvent changes, minimizing the amount of sample necessary and to ensuring maximal compatibility between the different techniques/strategies used for each particular PTM enrichment. The ultimate result of the development of these integrated techniques will be increasing the dimensional space of the analysis of biomedical problems by achieving maximum depth of analysis for single PTMs and incorporating multiple PTMs into the data matrix. This will facilitate the integration of data into pathways to achieve a systems biology view of the problem, and understanding of the inter-related role of multiple PTMs. This work was supported by the Dr. Miriam and Sheldon G. Stedman Nutrition and Metabolism Center, Duke University School of Medicine, Durham, NC, USA Data-independent acquisition (DIA) is an increasingly utilized method for peptide identification and quantification by mass spectrometry. Identification of peptides by DIA requires a spectral library, usually from past or parallel sample analysis using data-dependent acquisition (DDA). This approach is especially beneficial when there is no pre-existing spectral library, which is often the case in studies of novel PTMs, and when studies require many replicates or when sample quantity is limiting. In this work, we used PIQED to identify and quantify site-level acetylation and succinylation changes in mouse liver mitochondria proteins induced by six different diets collected after 2 weeks or 10 weeks, for a total of 12 dietary conditions: (1) chow control, (2) chow + fructose, (3) chow + glucose, (4) high-fat diet (HFD), (5) HFD + fructose, or (6) HFD + glucose. In parallel, we measured changes in mitochondrial protein quantities using Spectronaut. We find that many protein-level changes occur in mitochondrial-associated ribosomal proteins, as well as proteins involved in lipid/hormone metabolism. At the modification level, alterations in protein acetylation are more common than protein succinylation. Wiita University of California, San Francisco, CA, USA Copy number variation (CNV) in the genome, due to gains or losses of specific DNA regions, can be causative of human disease. However, unlike single gene disorders, CNV-associated syndromes can arise from complex underlying genetic bases that translate to diverse phenotypic outcomes that are not fully understood. Recently, CRISPR/Cas9 has been employed to engineer CNVs up to 2 Mb to study implications of these structural changes (Kraft et al. Cell Rep (2015) 10:833), but it remains unclear if engineering larger CNVs is feasible. As a proof-of-principle, we sought to develop an isogenic model of the 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (DS), the most common microdeletion disorder in humans. The 22q11.2 locus is highly susceptible to genomic rearrangements due to the presence of low copy repeats (LCR), with 85% of 22q11.2DS patients carrying a single-copy nearly 3-Mb deletion flanked by the two repeat regions LCR22A and LCR22D. Using a recently-described strategy (Tai et al. Nat Neurosci (2016) 19:517), we took advantage of these regions of nearly-identical sequence to design a single guide that targets both LCRs simultaneously to generate the microdeletion via non-homologous end joining on the resulting breakpoints. In initial gene dosage screening by qPCR, we achieved an encouraging success rate of nine out of 44 (20%) isogenic HEK293T clones harboring the deletion. We further validated the designed deletion by SNP microarray. Our initial goals in generating this model were to investigate 1) whether quantitative proteomics could distinguish protein level changes across this deleted region versus WT cells, pointing to a potential role in diagnostic evaluation and 2) whether individual clones harboring the same genetic deletion exhibit variability at the level of protein abundance, either expressed within the deleted locus or elsewhere in the genome, analogous to the variable phenotypic penetrance found in 22q11.2DS patients. We therefore characterized three deletion-positive clones using label-free quantitative proteomics. Our single-shot analysis on a Thermo Q-Exactive Plus over a 3.5 hour LC gradient detected nine of 43 annotated proteins mapped to the CNV region. As expected, we found a significant decrease in the mean expression of proteins encoded in the deletion locus, with moderate clone-to-clone variation, compared to the mean expression of other genes on Chr22 as well as across the genome. To varying degrees, all nine proteins exhibited lower average abundances in the clonal population when compared to the WT, suggesting that label-free quantification can detect these relatively subtle protein-level changes (predicted 33% decrease in HEK293T cells). However, label-free quantitative proteomics could not distinguish statistically significant changes elsewhere in the proteome that may relate to the phenotypic changes in 22q11.2DS. Taken together, we show that the single guide strategy can efficiently generate CNVs up to ∼3 Mb. These approaches can be used for downstream functional and proteomic studies, in more clinically relevant stem cell and murine models, to better dissect the spectrum of effects of syndromic CNVs.
